comment: Every place a source is weaker than it looks, and every place this package deliberately claims nothing. The facts themselves live in hardware.json; this file is about their standing, and it is the file a reader of any sibling repository looks in for that.

sources.corpus: conformance/corpus.json, recorded from an emulator named in pinned.json. Good evidence for behaviour nobody documented, poor evidence for anything a manufacturer printed.
sources.artifact: The firmware images themselves, which corroborate a size when a wrong size would fail to load.

divergences.topic: There is no document for the uPD96050.
divergences.documentSays: Nothing. No manufacturer document for this part was located.
divergences.referenceDoes: Secondary sources give 16384 program words, 2048 data ROM words, 2048 data RAM words and eight stack levels.
divergences.reasoning: Secondary sources for this family are emulators, which is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a fact a manufacturer would have printed. Three of the four figures have a second witness that is not an emulator: a published image for the larger part is exactly 16384 program words of three bytes plus 2048 table words of two bytes, so a wrong size would fail to load it. The stack depth has no such witness and rests on the secondary source alone.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: An NEC data sheet for the uPD96050, or a measurement: push past eight levels on a real part and see where it wraps. For the program side alone, a run of the second image that records its stack pointer over every command it accepts would bound it the way the census bounds the first.
divergences.census: conformance/stack.py walks every path a published image for the larger part can take from reset and from the interrupt vector, without running it. The image whose SHA-256 begins 55c697e864562445 reaches 533 words from reset, calls one level deep, never sets the interrupt enable bit and jumps through no register, so it needs one of the eight levels. The image whose SHA-256 begins 651b82a1e26c4fa8 jumps through the output register at address 13H, to a word it reads from its table at an index the host's data supplies, so a static walk stops there after 110 words and gives that image no bound. This bounds what one program needs. It says nothing about how deep the part's stack is.

divergences.topic: Every flag rule the data sheet does not state.
divergences.documentSays: Widths, stack depth, cycles per instruction and memory sizes for the uPD77C25. It does not specify every flag rule, every undefined encoding, or the result of every field combination.
divergences.referenceDoes: Answers all of those, because a recording answers whatever it was asked.
divergences.reasoning: Instruction-level behaviour the data sheet leaves open is taken from the recording, and the recording is an emulator. Where the two overlap the document wins and the recording is retaken; where they do not overlap there is nothing to check the recording against, and that covers most of the flag rules.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: A recording taken off a real uPD77C25: drive known inputs through a known program and capture the outputs. Failing that, a fuller NEC document than the Advance Product Information sheet.
divergences.narrowedBy: Table 6 of the 1989 data book states, for all sixteen ALU operations, which flags are affected, which are reset, which are held and which are indefinite. That is the manufacturer on behaviour this project had taken from the recording, and the model agrees with it on every cell: conformance/alu_flags.test.py drives all sixteen. What the recording still carries alone is the exact value of each affected flag, the auxiliary sign the manufacturer calls indefinite, and what a multi-bit shift brings in at the bottom.

divergences.topic: The two parts are treated as one instruction set with different sizes.
divergences.documentSays: The uPD77C25 and uPD77P25 are functionally identical, one mask ROM and one UVEPROM.
divergences.referenceDoes: Treats the uPD96050 as the same instruction set with more memory.
divergences.reasoning: The instruction set is modelled once and the sizes differ per model. That is a decision this package makes rather than a fact either source states, and it would be wrong if the larger part turned out to differ in behaviour rather than only in capacity.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: The missing uPD96050 data sheet, which would either confirm the instruction set or name a difference.

divergences.topic: How many cycles a reset costs.
divergences.documentSays: That a reset happens and what it leaves behind, and nothing about how long it takes. The pin gets one sentence.
divergences.referenceDoes: Nothing to compare against: the corpus records instruction behaviour and never resets the part.
divergences.reasoning: reset() spends no cycles. That is not a claim that a reset is instantaneous, which no silicon is; it is the absence of a figure. Spending a plausible number would put an invented one into every tally that crosses a reset, and a caller pacing against a wall would be pacing partly against this package's guess.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: A timing figure for the reset pin in an NEC document, or a measurement on a real part: hold the pin low, release it, and count clocks until the first program fetch.
divergences.settledBy: The 1989 data book's Interrupt Reset Timing Requirements give the reset pin a minimum pulse width of four clock cycles, and one clock cycle is one instruction on this part. reset() spends four. That is the minimum required of the host rather than a count of internal work, which the document still does not give, and the record says so beside the figure.
divergences.wouldReopenIt: An NEC document giving the part's internal reset sequence, which might be longer than the pulse the host has to supply.

divergences.topic: What a two-bit and a four-bit left shift bring in at the bottom.
divergences.documentSays: Table 6 names them a 2-bit left shift and a 4-bit left shift and says nothing about what arrives in the vacated bits.
divergences.referenceDoes: Brings ones in, so the result of either can never be zero.
divergences.reasoning: Following the recording here is visible rather than hidden: it makes the zero flag unreachable for those two operations, while the manufacturer's table marks that flag as derived from the result. Both statements can be true at once, and they are, but the reason the flag never fires is a choice taken from an emulator.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: A sentence in an NEC document about what a multi-bit shift shifts in, or a measurement on a real part: shift a known value and read the low bits back.

divergences.topic: When the serial input acknowledge rises and what lowers it.
divergences.documentSays: Figure 11 of the data book draws SIAK rising after the last bit has been clocked in and falling during the instruction its note marks, a move from SI, and the note's first line says that move sets the flag. Figure 2 draws SI ACK rising after SI Load, about half a serial clock after the last bit, where Figure 11 draws it about one serial clock after.
divergences.referenceDoes: Nothing: the emulator the corpus came from never sets or clears either acknowledge.
divergences.reasoning: The two waveforms agree that a whole word arriving raises the flag and a move from SI lowers it, and the model takes that. It raises the flag at the sample that sees the last bit's rising edge, which is the earliest the drawings allow. The note's first line contradicts the waveform beside it, and the delay between the edge and the flag differs between the two figures by up to one serial clock, so neither the wording nor the exact clock is settled.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: A measurement on a real part: clock a word in and poll JSIAK every instruction, then move from SI and poll again.

divergences.topic: Which half of a sixteen-bit serial register an eight-bit word occupies.
divergences.documentSays: That SIC and SOC select 8-bit or 16-bit transfers, that SIM puts the first bit at the MSB and SIL bit reverses it, and that SOM sends the MSB first. It does not say which bits of the sixteen-bit register an eight-bit word uses, nor what the other eight hold.
divergences.referenceDoes: Nothing: the emulator the corpus came from moves no serial bits.
divergences.reasoning: The model places an eight-bit word in the low byte: an arriving one lands there with the high byte cleared, SIL reverses only the low byte and leaves the high byte as it was, and SOM sends bit 7 first. That is a choice this package makes, and a part that used the high byte would read every eight-bit word differently.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: A measurement on a real part: in 8-bit mode, clock in a known byte and move SI to an accumulator, then load SO with a word whose two bytes differ and watch which byte leaves.

divergences.topic: What the serial shift registers hold at power on and after a reset.
divergences.documentSays: That RST initializes the internal logic and sets the program counter to 0. It does not list what else the reset sets, and says nothing about the shift registers or their bit counts.
divergences.referenceDoes: Nothing: the emulator the corpus came from has no shift registers.
divergences.reasoning: The shift registers and the count of bits each holds come up from the seed, as every other register does, and reset() leaves them alone because the only thing the document says a reset sets is the program counter. A host that needs a clean word boundary sets the counts itself, as the README's example does.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: A measurement on a real part: after power on, and again after a reset, clock a known word in and see whether it arrives whole.
